Kootenai Tribe of Idaho

The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho is a separately governed community within the wider Ktunaxa world. Its public history, dated constitutional publication and resource-restoration materials provide three complementary starting points. They connect remaining in Idaho and political organization with continuing responsibilities to the Kootenai River and its living resources.

Modern public-refuge wetland scene in the Kootenai River valley near Bonners Ferry, Idaho. The Kootenai Tribe of Idaho’s history places its continuing community and allotments along the Kootenai River and surrounding uplands. The FWS refuge account locates the photographed facility near Bonners Ferry, adjacent to the river’s west banks. This supports narrow Idaho regional/environmental context in the broader cross-border Kootenai/Ktunaxa collection; the photograph is not a picture of tribal members, reservation land, an identified cultural site, all Ktunaxa communities or a homeland boundary. The relationship comes from those inspected accounts, not merely the refuge sharing the name Kootenai. No legal rights or jurisdiction determination is made. These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Remaining in Idaho and organizing

The Tribe's history recounts pressure to relocate to Montana, continued residence near Bonners Ferry and peaceful protest in 1974 over neglect and inadequate living conditions. It is the Idaho community's own account of dispossession and self-determination. That specific history should remain distinct from the histories of other Ktunaxa governments across the international border and in Montana.

Read the sources [1] Kootenai Tribe of Idaho

02

A dated constitutional framework

The Tribe-hosted Constitution and Bylaws records adoption on April 10, 1947, and federal approval on June 16. Its compilation labels the latest amendment 1996. The text describes a Tribal Council able to represent the Tribe, manage its affairs and establish a court and law code. This dated framework does not independently establish every present amendment or current legal rule.

Read the sources [2] Kootenai Tribe of Idaho; original approval reproduced in the publication

03

River habitat and living resources

The Tribe's habitat-restoration and aquaculture accounts connect environmental change with habitat and subsistence concerns. They explain institutional priorities and related restoration work rather than simply listing offices. Read the program collection as a Tribal account of work and aspirations. It does not independently measure species recovery, prove every project outcome or supply an unchanged schedule for future work.

Read the sources [3] Kootenai Tribe of Idaho

Tribal History — Kootenai Tribe of Idaho ↗

Publication: Undated narrative; 2025 text copyright and 2026 site footer are not established publication dates

The Idaho Tribe's own substantial history distinguishes its community from other Ktunaxa bands and recounts relocation pressures and peaceful protest. It is an attributed community account, without independent review of every underlying treaty or administrative record.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual complete history body, lines 55–92, read. Synthesis selects relocation, continued Idaho residence and 1974 protest; belief narratives, numbers, private family detail and current compact terms excluded.

Review recorded: October 21, 2026

Constitution and Bylaws of the Kootenai Tribe of Idaho — dated compilation ↗

Publication: Compilation header: original approved 1947, latest amendment 1996. Certificate: adopted April 10, 1947; federal approval June 16, 1947. Compilation publication date unstated

The Tribe-hosted primary text supplies a dated institutional framework. Its header labels the latest amendment 1996; that is not verification of all current law. Adoption and federal approval dates are distinct; membership terms are not summarized.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual five-page text read, including preamble, Council provisions and adoption/approval certificates. Claim uses pages 1–2 and 4–5; no original amendment instruments independently inspected.
